summary:
The Central African Republic is dangerous for trans visitors.

Nothing in national law protects a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor. The constitution defines marriage as a union between one man and one woman and same-sex marriage is banned, so a visitor travelling with a partner has no recognition of that relationship, and affection between same-sex partners in public can be prosecuted under the public-morals provisions.

Consensual same-sex relations between adults are not explicitly criminalised in the penal code. Article 85 instead criminalises attacks on public morals, and same-sex conduct in public draws harsher penalties than other offences covered by the same moral-offence provisions. The practical effect for a visitor is that any visible same-sex or gender-nonconforming conduct in public exposes them to arrest on morals grounds.

The United States State Department's 2023 human rights report states that same-sex activity in public is criminalised in practice and that this treatment has pushed the affected community underground. The same report records that there were no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights in the country, so a visitor who faces trouble has no established local support network to turn to.

Legal gender recognition is not permitted in the Central African Republic. A visitor whose passport or identity marker does not match their presentation has no local legal route to align those documents, and should expect identity screening to proceed on the marker as issued.

Detention carries serious physical risk. Documentation from 2012 recorded extrajudicial killings, torture and rape by security forces and by Seleka rebels, together with harsh prison conditions. That reporting is more than a decade old and contains little trans-specific material, but it describes the conditions a visitor would enter if arrested on public-morals grounds.

The social climate compounds the legal exposure. Attitudes toward sexual orientation and gender identity issues are treated as taboo and characterised as imported from Europe or contrary to African values, which raises the likelihood of hostility from the public as well as from officials.
tangentialFactors:
The country has engaged with the international review mechanism on these questions. It received two Universal Periodic Review recommendations concerning non-discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and improving the situation of sexual minorities, and the January 2024 United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights summary of stakeholder submissions for the country's 45th-session review again contains SOGI-related recommendations. Whether any of these recommendations have been implemented is not sourced here.

The Central African Republic appears in ILGA World's 2023 survey of laws criminalising LGBT people, but the underlying national position is narrower than that inclusion suggests: consensual same-sex relations are not expressly prohibited, while exposure arises from the public-morals offence rather than a specific sodomy statute.

The 2012 human rights reporting that documents state violence also covers armed-group violence during the Seleka period, an environment of general instability in which a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner has no special status or protection.
localsOnly:
Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity; the United States State Department's 2023 report confirms the absence of legal anti-discrimination provisions for LGBTQI+ persons.

LGBTQI+ persons cannot serve openly in the Central African Republic's armed forces.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable, so residents have no administrative procedure to change the sex marker on identity documents.

There were no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights operating in the country as of the 2023 reporting, and the affected community is described as having been driven underground by enforcement of the public-morals offence.

Residents seeking change must work through the Universal Periodic Review process, where two earlier recommendations on SOGI non-discrimination and the situation of sexual minorities, and further stakeholder recommendations in the January 2024 submissions, form the documented record of external pressure.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on the criminalisation question and this is unresolved. The 2019 overview states that same-sex relations between consenting adults are not explicitly criminalised, relying on Article 85's public-morals offence, whereas the 2023 United States State Department report describes same-sex activity in public as criminalised. The distinction between a specific offence and enforcement through the morals provision is not settled by the available material.

No source in the inventory documents arrests, prosecutions or sentences under Article 85, so the frequency and severity of enforcement are not sourced. Likewise there is no sourced information on hate-crime sentencing, on access to healthcare for trans visitors, or on airport and border screening practices directed at gender-nonconforming travellers.

The 2012 documentation of killings, torture, rape and prison conditions derives from a period of armed conflict and is not trans-specific; its current applicability to detention of a trans visitor is not verified. The 2024 Universal Periodic Review stakeholder submissions and the two earlier recommendations are recorded as inputs to the review process only, with no sourced outcome as to implementation.
